questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball strikes a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 10 m/s. The magnitude of the impulse on the ball is
questions.e: Taking the rebound as negative, Δp = 0.2 × (10 − (−10)) = 4 N·s. A common slip is to subtract the speeds and get zero, forgetting that velocity reverses.

questions.s: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force on the body is directed
o: towards the centre of the circle
questions.e: The force changing the direction of velocity must point inwards. Away from the centre describes the so-called centrifugal effect, which is not a real force in an inertial frame.

questions.s: A motor lifts a 60 kg load through 20 m in 40 s at constant speed. Taking g = 10 m/s², its useful power output is
questions.e: Work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 20 = 12,000 J, and P = W/t = 12,000/40 = 300 W. 12,000 is the work, not the power.

questions.s: For a projectile launched at an angle on level ground, the range is greatest, for a fixed launch speed and no air resistance, when the angle is
questions.e: R = u² sin2θ/g is maximum when sin2θ = 1, that is θ = 45°. At 90° the projectile goes straight up and its range is zero.

questions.s: A wheel rotates at 120 revolutions per minute. Its angular speed in rad/s is
questions.e: 120 rev/min = 2 rev/s, and each revolution is 2π rad, so ω = 4π rad/s. 240π results from multiplying by 2π without dividing by 60.

questions.s: Kepler's second law, that a line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, is a consequence of the conservation of
questions.e: The Sun's pull is central, so it exerts no torque about the Sun, and the planet's angular momentum is constant. The planet therefore moves faster when nearer to the Sun.

questions.s: A force of 50 N pulls a trolley 10 m along the ground, with the force making an angle of 60° with the direction of motion. The work done is
questions.e: W = Fd cosθ = 50 × 10 × 0.5 = 250 J. 500 J ignores the angle, and 433 J uses sin60° instead of cos60°.

questions.s: The surface escape speed of a planet is v. A second planet has the same radius but four times the mass. Its escape speed is
questions.e: vₑ = √(2GM/R) ∝ √M at fixed radius, so quadrupling the mass doubles vₑ. The speed is not proportional to M itself.

questions.s: Which one of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.e: Displacement has magnitude and direction. Work, speed and power are scalars; speed is only the magnitude of velocity.

questions.s: Two vectors have magnitudes 4 and 5 and the angle between them is 30°. The magnitude of their vector product is
questions.e: |A × B| = AB sinθ = 4 × 5 × ½ = 10. 17.3 comes from using cos30°, which gives the scalar product.

questions.s: According to Bernoulli's principle, in a horizontal pipe carrying an ideal fluid, the pressure is lowest where
questions.e: P + ½ρv² is constant along a streamline, so a higher speed means a lower pressure. The narrow section of a pipe has the highest speed.

questions.s: One watt is equal to
questions.e: Power = energy/time, so 1 W = 1 J/s. A newton metre is also a joule, but that is energy, not power.

questions.s: The slope of a velocity–time graph at any instant gives the body's
questions.e: Slope = Δv/Δt, which is acceleration. Displacement is the area under the graph, not its slope.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m at a constant speed of 4 m/s. The tension in the string is
questions.e: T = mv²/r = 0.5 × 16/2 = 4 N. Using mv² without dividing by r gives 8 N, and using mv/r gives 1 N.

questions.s: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.e: a = (v − u)/t = (30 − 10)/5 = 4 m/s². Adding the speeds (40/5 = 8) is the common slip; acceleration depends on the change in velocity.

questions.s: For the same two surfaces, the limiting static friction compared with the kinetic friction is generally
questions.e: It takes a larger force to start a body moving than to keep it moving, so μₛ > μₖ.

questions.s: The gauge pressure at a depth of 5 m in fresh water of density 1,000 kg/m³ is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: P = ρgh = 1,000 × 10 × 5 = 50,000 Pa. Leaving out g gives 5,000, and adding atmospheric pressure is not part of gauge pressure.

questions.s: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 6 m/s?
questions.e: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 36 = 36 J. Omitting the square gives 6 J and omitting the ½ gives 72 J.

questions.s: A force of 20 N acts perpendicular to a spanner at a distance of 0.3 m from the nut. The torque about the nut is
questions.e: τ = rF sinθ = 0.3 × 20 × 1 = 6 N·m. 60 N·m comes from a decimal-place slip, and 0.015 from dividing the distance by the force.

questions.s: A small steel ball falls through a viscous liquid and reaches terminal velocity. At that stage
o: the ball has stopped accelerating because gravity vanishes
the viscous force is less than the weight
the net force on the ball is zero
questions.e: At terminal speed, weight = upthrust + viscous drag, so the net force is zero and the speed is constant. Gravity continues to act.

questions.s: A moving ball collides head-on elastically with an identical ball at rest. Afterwards
o: the first ball stops and the second moves with the first ball's original velocity
both balls move with half the original velocity
the first ball continues at the same velocity
questions.e: For equal masses in a head-on elastic collision, velocities are exchanged. Conserving both momentum and kinetic energy rules out the other outcomes.

questions.s: A skater spinning at 2 rad/s with moment of inertia 4 kg·m² pulls in her arms so that her moment of inertia becomes 1 kg·m². Her new angular speed is
questions.e: Angular momentum is conserved: 4 × 2 = 1 × ω, so ω = 8 rad/s. Reducing I raises ω, so 0.5 rad/s (the inverted ratio) cannot be right.

questions.s: A rocket moves forward because
o: the exhaust pushes against the surrounding air
the exhaust gases carry momentum backwards, so the rocket gains equal momentum forward
its engine reduces its mass only
questions.e: It is momentum conservation (equivalent to Newton's third law), which is why rockets work in vacuum, where there is no air to push against.

questions.s: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a 4 kg trolley at rest and they stick together. Their common speed is
questions.e: Momentum is conserved: 2 × 3 = (2 + 4)v, so v = 1 m/s. Using only the 2 kg mass in the denominator gives 3 m/s, which would mean no change.

questions.s: The escape velocity of an object from the Earth's surface depends on
o: the mass and radius of the Earth, but not on the mass of the object
the direction in which it is launched
questions.e: vₑ = √(2GM/R) contains no term for the object's own mass.

questions.s: A satellite A orbits a planet at radius r and satellite B at radius 4r. The ratio of the period of B to that of A is
questions.e: Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2) = 4^(3/2) = 8. Ratios of 4 or 2 come from using T ∝ r or T ∝ √r.

questions.s: A passenger standing in a bus is thrown forward when the bus brakes suddenly. This is best explained by
questions.e: The passenger tends to keep moving at the earlier velocity, which is inertia. The third law concerns action and reaction pairs acting on different bodies.

questions.s: A body starts with a speed of 5 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 4 s. How far does it travel?
questions.e: s = ut + ½at² = 5(4) + ½(2)(16) = 20 + 16 = 36 m. Omitting the ½ gives 52 m, and using only ut gives 20 m.

questions.s: The orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit around the Earth is independent of
questions.e: Equating GMm/r² to mv²/r, the satellite mass m cancels, leaving v = √(GM/r).

questions.s: The acceleration due to gravity on the Earth's surface is 10 m/s². At a height equal to the Earth's radius above the surface it is
questions.e: The distance from the centre is 2R, and g ∝ 1/r², so g′ = 10/4 = 2.5 m/s². Halving (5 m/s²) wrongly treats g as ∝ 1/r.

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. The work done on it by the gravitational force during one revolution is
o: positive and equal to its kinetic energy
negative and equal to its potential energy
equal to mg times the orbital radius
questions.e: The gravitational force always acts at 90° to the displacement, so W = Fd cos90° = 0. This is why the orbital speed stays constant.

questions.s: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², its speed on reaching the ground is
questions.e: mgh = ½mv² gives v = √(2gh) = √400 = 20 m/s. Leaving out the factor 2 gives √200 ≈ 14 m/s.

questions.s: The moment of inertia of a rigid body about an axis depends on
o: its mass distribution relative to the axis
questions.e: I = Σmr², so the same body has different values for different axes. It is a property of the body and axis, not of the motion.

questions.s: In a hydraulic press the small piston has an area of 2 cm² and the large piston 100 cm². A force of 100 N acts on the small piston. The force on the large piston is
questions.e: Pressure is transmitted equally: F₂ = F₁(A₂/A₁) = 100 × 50 = 5,000 N. Inverting the ratio would give only 2 N, and 200 N results from multiplying by the small area instead of dividing.

questions.s: A uniform seesaw has a girl of mass 40 kg sitting 1.5 m from the pivot. A boy sits on the other side, 2 m from the pivot, and it balances. The boy's mass is
questions.e: Equal torques: 40 × 1.5 = m × 2, so m = 30 kg. Inverting the distances gives 53 kg.

questions.s: Masses of 3 kg and 5 kg hang from the two ends of a light string over a smooth light pulley. Taking g = 10 m/s², the acceleration of the masses is
questions.e: a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (2 × 10)/8 = 2.5 m/s². Dividing by only one mass, or forgetting to add the masses in the denominator, gives wrong values such as 5 m/s².

questions.s: A ball is projected at 30 m/s at 45° to the horizontal on level ground. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is its horizontal range?
questions.e: R = u² sin2θ/g = 900 × sin 90°/10 = 90 m. Using sinθ in place of sin2θ gives about 64 m, and 180 m results from omitting the division by g = 10 and halving.

questions.s: A 5 kg load is lifted 12 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s², its gain in gravitational potential energy is
questions.e: ΔPE = mgh = 5 × 10 × 12 = 600 J. Halving it (300 J) wrongly treats it like kinetic energy.

questions.s: At the highest point of its path, a projectile (no air resistance) has
o: zero horizontal velocity and acceleration g downwards
zero vertical velocity and acceleration g downwards
questions.e: Only the vertical component vanishes at the top; the horizontal component stays constant. Gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g downwards all the time.

questions.s: One newton has the same unit as
o: the rate of change of momentum
the rate of change of energy
the product of mass and velocity
the product of pressure and volume
questions.e: F = Δp/Δt, so force and momentum per second share the unit kg·m/s². Mass × velocity is momentum itself, pressure × volume is energy, and energy per second is power.

questions.s: A force is conservative if the work it does on a body moving between two points
o: is always equal to the change in momentum
is independent of the path taken
questions.e: Gravity and the spring force are examples; friction is not, since its work depends on the path length.

questions.s: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body at right angles to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.e: R = √(3² + 4²) = 5 N. The sum 7 N applies only when the forces act in the same direction.

questions.s: A 20 kg crate rests on a rough floor where the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.4. Taking g = 10 m/s², the friction force while it slides is
questions.e: f = μN = 0.4 × (20 × 10) = 80 N. 200 N is the weight, and 8 N results from using N = mg/g.

questions.s: In a perfectly inelastic collision between two bodies on a smooth surface, which quantity is conserved?
questions.e: Momentum is conserved in every collision when no external force acts. Some kinetic energy is lost as heat and sound, and the bodies move off together.

questions.s: A 5 kg block slides down a smooth (frictionless) plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its acceleration is
questions.e: Along the plane a = g sinθ = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s², independent of mass. g cosθ = 8.7 m/s² is the component perpendicular to the plane.

questions.s: A projectile is fired at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its maximum height is
questions.e: The vertical component is 20 sin30° = 10 m/s, so H = (10)²/(2 × 10) = 5 m. Using the full speed 20 m/s gives 20 m.

questions.s: A geostationary satellite has an orbital period of
questions.e: It must complete one orbit in the time the Earth turns once so that it stays above the same point on the equator.

questions.s: A car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest with a constant deceleration of 5 m/s². The stopping distance is
questions.e: v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 400 − 10s, so s = 40 m. 80 m comes from omitting the 2 in 2as.

questions.s: A car rounds a flat circular bend of radius 20 m. If the coefficient of friction between tyres and road is 0.5 and g = 10 m/s², the maximum safe speed is
questions.e: Friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r, so v = √(μgr) = √(0.5 × 10 × 20) = √100 = 10 m/s. Forgetting the square root gives 100.

questions.s: Water flows at 2 m/s through a pipe of cross-section 4 cm². The pipe narrows to 1 cm². The speed of the water in the narrow part is
questions.e: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₂ = 4 × 2/1 = 8 m/s. 0.5 m/s results from inverting the area ratio.

questions.s: A stone is dropped from rest from a bridge. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is its speed after 3 s?
questions.e: v = u + gt = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m/s. 45 m is the distance fallen (½gt²), not a speed.

questions.s: The scalar product of two non-zero vectors is zero when the angle between them is
questions.e: A·B = AB cosθ, which is zero only for θ = 90°. At 0° and 180° it takes its largest magnitudes, +AB and −AB.

questions.s: Archimedes' principle states that the upthrust on a body immersed in a fluid equals
o: the weight of the fluid displaced by the body
questions.e: Upthrust is the weight of displaced fluid. It equals the body's weight only when the body floats freely.

questions.s: A projectile is fired at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal from level ground. Taking g = 10 m/s², its time of flight is
questions.e: T = 2u sinθ/g = 2 × 20 × 0.5/10 = 2 s. Using cosθ instead gives about 3.5 s, and 1 s is only the time to the top.

questions.s: A block of volume 0.002 m³ is completely submerged in water (density 1,000 kg/m³). Taking g = 10 m/s², the buoyant force on it is
questions.e: Buoyant force = ρVg = 1,000 × 0.002 × 10 = 20 N, the weight of water displaced. It does not depend on the block's own mass.

questions.s: A 2 kg mass is placed at x = 0 and a 3 kg mass at x = 5 m. The centre of mass lies at
questions.e: x = (2 × 0 + 3 × 5)/(2 + 3) = 3 m, nearer the heavier mass. The midpoint 2.5 m is correct only for equal masses.

questions.s: An astronaut inside a satellite orbiting the Earth feels weightless because
o: there is no gravity at that height
the Earth's pull is cancelled by the Moon
the satellite is outside the atmosphere
she and the satellite are both in free fall with the same acceleration
questions.e: Gravity is still strong at orbital heights; both fall towards the Earth with the same acceleration, so there is no contact force between them.

questions.s: The area under a force–time graph for a body represents
questions.e: ∫F dt = impulse = change in momentum. The area under a force–distance graph is the work done.

questions.s: A small sphere falls through a viscous fluid. According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag on it, at low speed, is proportional to
o: its radius squared and its speed
its mass and the square of its speed
the square of its radius only
questions.e: F = 6πηrv, so it varies linearly with both r and v. Drag proportional to v² is the model for fast turbulent motion.

questions.s: A uniform solid disc and a hoop of the same mass and radius are released together from rest at the top of a rough incline and roll without slipping. Which statement is correct?
o: The disc reaches the bottom first
The hoop reaches the bottom first
The result depends on their common mass
questions.e: The hoop has a larger moment of inertia (mr²) than the disc (½mr²), so more of its energy goes into rotation and it accelerates less. Mass cancels out, so it does not affect the outcome.

questions.s: A particle in SHM has angular frequency 10 rad/s and amplitude 5 cm. When its displacement from the mean position is 3 cm, its speed is
questions.e: v = ω√(A² − x²) = 10 × √(25 − 9) = 10 × 4 = 40 cm/s. 50 cm/s is the maximum speed at x = 0, and 30 cm/s uses ωx.

questions.s: In a stationary wave on a string fixed at both ends, the points of zero amplitude are called
questions.e: Nodes are permanently at rest; antinodes have maximum amplitude, and are halfway between neighbouring nodes.

questions.s: A sound's intensity increases by a factor of 100. By how many decibels does its level increase?
questions.e: Δβ = 10 log 100 = 10 × 2 = 20 dB. The level scale is logarithmic, so a hundred-fold increase does not add 100 dB.

questions.s: A body executes SHM with amplitude 5 cm and frequency 2 Hz. Its maximum speed is approximately
questions.e: ω = 2πf = 4π rad/s and vmax = ωA = 4π × 0.05 = 0.628 m/s. Using A in centimetres without conversion would give 63 'm/s'; 0.31 results from omitting a factor of 2 in ω.

questions.s: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats heard per second is
questions.e: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies, 260 − 256 = 4 Hz. 516 is their sum, which has no meaning here.

questions.s: A closed organ pipe of length 0.5 m is sounded in its fundamental mode. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, the frequency is
questions.e: A closed pipe has a node at one end and an antinode at the other, so λ = 4L = 2 m and f = 340/2 = 170 Hz. 340 Hz would apply to an open pipe.

questions.s: In a body executing SHM, the period is
o: proportional to the square of the amplitude
questions.e: T = 2π√(m/k) contains no amplitude term, which is why a clock pendulum keeps time even as its swing dies down slightly.

questions.s: A siren moving away from a stationary observer produces a note that the observer hears as
o: higher in frequency than the siren emits
the same as the siren emits
lower in frequency than the siren emits
questions.e: The waves are stretched behind the source, so the received wavelength is longer and frequency lower.

questions.s: The threshold of hearing is I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m². The intensity level of a sound of intensity 10⁻⁶ W/m² is
questions.e: β = 10 log(I/I₀) = 10 log(10⁶) = 60 dB. 120 dB would result from multiplying the exponent by 2.

questions.s: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration is
o: proportional to the displacement and directed away from the mean position
proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position
questions.e: a = −ω²x: the restoring acceleration points towards equilibrium and grows with displacement. A constant acceleration describes free fall, not SHM.

questions.s: Resonance occurs in a driven oscillating system when
o: the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system
the driving frequency is twice the natural frequency
questions.e: At resonance energy transfer is most efficient and the amplitude is greatest. Heavy damping reduces the peak, not raises it.

questions.s: Sound of frequency 256 Hz travels in air at 340 m/s. Its wavelength is approximately
questions.e: λ = v/f = 340/256 = 1.33 m. 0.75 m comes from inverting the ratio.

questions.s: A standing wave of wavelength 1.2 m is set up on a string. The distance between two adjacent nodes is
questions.e: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart: 1.2/2 = 0.6 m. A distance of λ/4 separates a node from its adjacent antinode.

questions.s: At the mean position of a body in SHM, its kinetic energy is
questions.e: At the mean position the speed is greatest and the potential energy is least, so KE equals the total energy.

questions.s: Ultrasonic waves are sound waves with a frequency
o: equal to the frequency of light
questions.e: Ultrasound lies above the upper limit of normal human hearing, about 20 kHz. Below 20 Hz is infrasound.

questions.s: A body in SHM has angular frequency 10 rad/s and amplitude 5 cm. Its maximum acceleration is
questions.e: a_max = ω²A = 100 × 0.05 = 5 m/s². Using ωA gives 0.5 m/s², which is the maximum speed.

questions.s: A mass on a spring of constant 200 N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. The total energy of the oscillation is
questions.e: E = ½kA² = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J. Using kA² without the ½ gives 2 J, and 20 J comes from kA, with A not squared and no ½.

questions.s: A simple pendulum is taken to a planet where the acceleration due to gravity is one quarter of that on Earth. Its period becomes
o: one quarter of that on Earth
questions.e: T ∝ 1/√g. With g reduced to g/4, T becomes 2T. Four times would hold only if T were ∝ 1/g.

questions.s: A stretched string of length 0.5 m, fixed at both ends, carries waves of speed 200 m/s. The frequency of its fundamental mode is
questions.e: For the fundamental, λ = 2L = 1 m, so f = v/λ = 200 Hz. Using λ = L gives 400 Hz.

questions.s: A travelling wave is described by y = 0.02 sin(4πx − 200πt), with x and y in metres and t in seconds. Its speed is
questions.e: v = ω/k = 200π/4π = 50 m/s. The frequency is 100 Hz and the wavelength 0.5 m, and 100 × 0.5 = 50 m/s as a check.

questions.s: A simple pendulum of length 2.5 m oscillates at a place where g = 10 m/s². Its time period is
questions.e: T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(0.25) = 2π × 0.5 = π ≈ 3.14 s. Forgetting the 2π, or not taking the square root, gives other values.

questions.s: The wavelength of a 20 Hz sound wave in air, where the speed of sound is 340 m/s, is
questions.e: λ = v/f = 340/20 = 17 m. This is the lowest audible frequency and has a very long wavelength.

questions.s: Sound travels fastest in
questions.e: Sound is fastest in solids because of their high elasticity; in steel it is more than ten times faster than in air. It cannot travel in a vacuum.

questions.s: Two waves of the same frequency and amplitude meet at a point with a path difference of λ/2. The resultant amplitude there is
questions.e: A path difference of λ/2 means a phase difference π, so crests meet troughs and the waves cancel. A path difference of λ gives the double amplitude.

questions.s: The pitch of a musical note depends mainly on its
questions.e: A higher frequency gives a higher pitch. Amplitude controls loudness and waveform controls quality (timbre).

questions.s: A closed organ pipe can sustain only
questions.e: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only odd multiples of the fundamental (1f, 3f, 5f) fit.

questions.s: A source emitting 600 Hz moves towards a stationary listener at 20 m/s. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. The frequency heard is
questions.e: f′ = f v/(v − vₛ) = 600 × 340/320 = 637.5 Hz. 567 Hz would be for a source moving away, using v + vₛ.

questions.s: The Doppler effect is observed when
o: there is relative motion between the source and the observer
the source and observer are at rest
two waves of equal frequency superpose
a wave enters a denser medium
questions.e: Relative motion changes the number of wave-crests received per second. It applies to sound and light alike.

questions.s: An open organ pipe of length 0.5 m is sounded in its fundamental mode. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, the frequency is
questions.e: For an open pipe f₁ = v/2L = 340/1 = 340 Hz. 170 Hz is the fundamental of a closed pipe of the same length.

questions.s: In SHM the total mechanical energy of an oscillator is
o: maximum at the mean position and zero at the ends
constant and proportional to the square of the amplitude
questions.e: KE and PE keep exchanging but their sum is ½kA², constant for an undamped system. Doubling A multiplies E by four.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg mass is attached to a light spring of force constant 200 N/m and set in SHM. Its time period is
questions.e: T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(0.5/200) = 2π × 0.05 = 0.314 s. 3.2 s is the frequency-like value 1/T, and 0.63 s comes from using √(m/k) × 4π.

questions.s: The length of a simple pendulum is increased to four times its original value. Its time period becomes
questions.e: T ∝ √L, so quadrupling L doubles T. The period does not depend on the bob's mass.

questions.s: A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Its speed is
questions.e: v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m/s. Dividing frequency by wavelength gives 735, which is not a speed.

questions.s: Sound waves in air are
questions.e: Air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions. Sound needs a material medium.

questions.s: A man hears the echo of his shout from a cliff 2 s after shouting. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, the cliff is how far away?
questions.e: The sound travels to the cliff and back, so 2d = 340 × 2 = 680 m and d = 340 m. 680 m is the total path.

questions.s: A listener moves towards a stationary source of frequency 500 Hz at 17 m/s. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. The frequency heard is
questions.e: f′ = f(v + v₀)/v = 500 × 357/340 = 525 Hz. A listener moving away would hear 475 Hz.

questions.s: In SHM the velocity is ahead of the displacement in phase by
questions.e: If x = A sinωt, then v = Aω cosωt, which leads x by a quarter of a cycle, π/2. The acceleration, not the velocity, is in antiphase with x.

questions.s: Beats are produced when two waves of
o: equal frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions
the same frequency are superposed in phase
questions.e: Their alternating constructive and destructive interference gives a periodic rise and fall of loudness at the difference frequency. Waves of equal frequency in opposite directions give a standing wave.

questions.s: A mass attached to a spring oscillates with period T. If the mass is quadrupled, the new period is
questions.e: T = 2π√(m/k) ∝ √m, so quadrupling m doubles T. 4T would imply T ∝ m.

questions.s: The speed of sound in a gas is directly proportional to the
o: square root of the absolute temperature
pressure of the gas at constant temperature
questions.e: v = √(γRT/M), so v ∝ √T. At constant temperature, a change of pressure alone has no effect on v.

questions.s: Absolute zero on the Celsius scale is approximately
questions.e: Absolute zero is 0 K, and since T(K) = t(°C) + 273 it lies at about −273 °C. −373 °C comes from subtracting 100 instead of 273.

questions.s: A sealed rigid vessel holds a gas at 2.0 atm and 27 °C. The vessel is heated to 127 °C. The pressure becomes about
questions.e: At constant volume p ∝ T (in kelvin): p₂ = 2.0 × 400/300 = 2.67 atm. Using the Celsius readings (2.0 × 127/27) would give 9.4 atm, which is wrong because the scale must start at absolute zero.

questions.s: At the same temperature, the ratio of the r.m.s. speed of hydrogen molecules (molar mass 2 g/mol) to that of oxygen molecules (32 g/mol) is
questions.e: v_rms = √(3RT/M), so v ∝ 1/√M. The ratio is √(32/2) = √16 = 4, so hydrogen is four times faster. 16 : 1 forgets the square root.

questions.s: Taking k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at 300 K is
questions.e: ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J. The value 4.1 × 10⁻²¹ J is kT alone, with the factor 3/2 missing.

questions.s: A Carnot engine works between a source at 500 K and a sink at 300 K. Its efficiency is
questions.e: η = 1 − T_c/T_h = 1 − 300/500 = 0.40. 60 % is the ratio T_c/T_h itself, and 167 % comes from inverting it; no engine can exceed 100 %.

questions.s: In a certain process a gas takes in 800 J of heat from its surroundings and expands, doing 300 J of work. The change in its internal energy is
questions.e: By the first law ΔU = Q − W = 800 − 300 = +500 J. +1,100 J would result from adding the work done by the gas instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: An ideal gas expands isothermally and absorbs 400 J of heat from a reservoir. The work done by the gas is
questions.e: For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature, so ΔU = 0 in an isothermal change and Q = W = 400 J. Zero work would hold only if the volume stayed fixed.

questions.s: A gas is compressed rapidly in a well-insulated cylinder, and 250 J of work is done on it. The change in its internal energy is
questions.e: Insulation means Q = 0, so ΔU = −W, where W = −250 J is the work done by the gas. Hence ΔU = +250 J and the gas warms up. 0 J would apply to an isothermal process.

questions.s: A gas at constant temperature has volume 2.0 L at 3.0 atm. It is compressed to 1.5 L. The new pressure is
questions.e: Boyle's law: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, so p₂ = 3.0 × 2.0/1.5 = 4.0 atm. 2.25 atm comes from multiplying by V₂/V₁ instead of V₁/V₂.

questions.s: A fixed mass of gas at constant pressure has volume 300 cm³ at 27 °C. Its volume at 127 °C is
questions.e: Charles's law: V/T is constant with T in kelvin, so V₂ = 300 × 400/300 = 400 cm³. Using Celsius values gives 1,414 cm³, which is not allowed.

questions.s: The specific heat capacity of water is 4,200 J/(kg K). The heat needed to warm 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C is
questions.e: Q = mcΔT = 2 × 4,200 × 50 = 4.2 × 10⁵ J. 2.1 × 10⁵ J forgets the mass of 2 kg.

questions.s: The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg. The heat needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice already at 0 °C is
questions.e: Q = mL = 0.50 × 3.36 × 10⁵ = 1.68 × 10⁵ J, with no change of temperature. 3.36 × 10⁵ J is the value for 1 kg.

questions.s: Which of the following is a statement of the second law of thermodynamics?
o: No cyclic engine can convert all the heat it absorbs into work
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
Bodies in thermal equilibrium with a third body are in equilibrium with each other
The entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at absolute zero
questions.e: The Kelvin–Planck form says that a heat engine working in a cycle must reject some heat to a colder sink. The other statements are the first law, the zeroth law and the third law respectively.

questions.s: Take R = 8.31 J/(mol K). The pressure of 2.0 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K in a vessel of volume 0.0249 m³ is about
questions.e: p = nRT/V = 2.0 × 8.31 × 300/0.0249 ≈ 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa results from taking n = 1 mol.

questions.s: A reservoir at a constant 300 K absorbs 600 J of heat reversibly. Its change of entropy is
questions.e: ΔS = Q/T = 600/300 = +2 J/K, positive because heat enters. +0.5 J/K comes from dividing the other way round.

questions.s: A reversible refrigerator keeps its cold space at 270 K and releases heat to a room at 300 K. Its coefficient of performance is
questions.e: COP = T_c/(T_h − T_c) = 270/30 = 9. 10 is T_h/(T_h − T_c), the figure for a heat pump, and 0.11 is the inverse of the correct value.

questions.s: A Carnot engine with its sink at 300 K has an efficiency of 25 %. By how many kelvin must the source temperature be raised to make the efficiency 40 %?
questions.e: For 25 %, T_h = 300/0.75 = 400 K; for 40 %, T_h = 300/0.60 = 500 K. The increase is 100 K. 60 K simply copies the 15 % rise in efficiency.

questions.s: A monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its volume. Its final temperature is
questions.e: TV^(γ−1) is constant: T₂ = 300 × 8^(2/3) = 300 × 4 = 1,200 K. 2,400 K results from multiplying by 8, which would be true only at constant pressure and amount.

questions.s: Take R = 8.31 J/(mol K). The heat needed to raise the temperature of 2.0 mol of a monatomic ideal gas by 50 K at constant pressure is about
questions.e: At constant pressure Q = nC_pΔT with C_p = (5/2)R: Q = 2 × 2.5 × 8.31 × 50 ≈ 2,078 J. 1,250 J uses C_v = (3/2)R, which applies at constant volume.

questions.s: 200 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with 300 g of water at 30 °C in an insulated container. Ignoring the container, the final temperature is
questions.e: Heat lost = heat gained: 200(80 − T) = 300(T − 30), so T = 25,000/500 = 50 °C. 55 °C is the plain average, which ignores the unequal masses.

questions.s: The normal human body temperature of 37 °C is equal to
questions.e: T(K) = t(°C) + 273 = 37 + 273 = 310 K. 236 K comes from subtracting instead of adding.

questions.s: For one mole of an ideal gas, the difference of the molar heat capacities C_p − C_v is equal to
questions.e: Heating at constant pressure also supplies the work of expansion, which for one mole is RΔT, so C_p − C_v = R (Mayer's relation).

questions.s: The ratio C_p/C_v for a monatomic ideal gas such as helium is
questions.e: A monatomic gas has three translational degrees of freedom: C_v = (3/2)R and C_p = (5/2)R, so γ = 5/3. 7/5 is the value for a diatomic gas.

questions.s: A gas at a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa expands from 0.010 m³ to 0.013 m³. The work done by the gas is
questions.e: W = pΔV = 2.0 × 10⁵ × 0.003 = 600 J. 6,000 J comes from using 0.03 m³ for the volume change.

questions.s: If body A is in thermal equilibrium with body C, and body B is also in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This statement is called the
questions.e: The zeroth law makes temperature a meaningful property: bodies with a common temperature stay in equilibrium when brought together.

questions.s: A Carnot engine operates between 1,000 K and 400 K. Its efficiency is
questions.e: η = 1 − 400/1,000 = 0.60. 40 % is the ratio T_c/T_h, which gives the fraction rejected, not converted.

questions.s: A heat engine takes in 800 J from its source in each cycle and does 200 J of work. The heat rejected to the sink per cycle is
questions.e: By energy conservation Q_c = Q_h − W = 800 − 200 = 600 J, and the efficiency is 25 %. 1,000 J adds the work instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: Take R = 8.31 J/(mol K). The internal energy of 2.0 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 K is about
questions.e: U = (3/2)nRT = 1.5 × 2 × 8.31 × 300 ≈ 7,479 J. 3.7 kJ is the value for 1 mol.

questions.s: A steel rod 2.0 m long has a linear expansion coefficient of 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. When its temperature rises by 50 K, its length increases by
questions.e: ΔL = αLΔT = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 2.0 × 50 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m = 1.2 mm. 2.4 mm doubles the length by mistake.

questions.s: The r.m.s. speed of nitrogen molecules at 27 °C is v. At 927 °C the r.m.s. speed is
questions.e: v ∝ √T with T in kelvin: T goes from 300 K to 1,200 K, so v becomes √4 = 2 times larger. Using the Celsius numbers gives an absurd factor of about 5.9.

questions.s: The SI unit of magnetic flux density is the
questions.e: One tesla equals one weber per square metre. The weber is the unit of flux itself.

questions.s: A capacitor in a DC circuit, once fully charged,
questions.e: With the capacitor charged, its voltage equals the supply and the current falls to zero. At AC it offers finite reactance instead.

questions.s: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of
questions.e: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. A kilowatt on its own is a unit of power.

questions.s: A proton (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a field of 0.1 T. The radius of its circular path is about
questions.e: r = mv/(qB) = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 10⁶/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.1) = 0.104 m. The radius is proportional to the speed and the mass.

questions.s: At the resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit, the current is
o: maximum and in phase with the supply voltage
minimum and in phase with the supply voltage
questions.e: At resonance X_L = X_C so Z = R, its minimum value, and the current V/R is largest. The reactances cancel, so the phase angle is zero.

questions.s: Inserting a dielectric slab between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor
o: increases the charge on the plates
has no effect on the capacitance
increases the electric field in the gap
decreases the potential difference across the plates
questions.e: The dielectric raises C by the factor K. With Q fixed, V = Q/C falls. The charge on an isolated capacitor cannot change.

questions.s: The energy stored in the magnetic field of an inductor of 2 H carrying 3 A is
questions.e: U = ½LI² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J. Without the ½ the result would be 18 J, and 6 J results from LI.

questions.s: A domestic AC supply has a peak voltage of about 311 V. Its r.m.s. value is about
questions.e: Vrms = V₀/√2 = 311/1.414 ≈ 220 V. 155 V comes from dividing by 2.

questions.s: An ideal voltmeter should have
o: a very low resistance and be connected in parallel
a very high resistance and be connected in series
a very high resistance and be connected in parallel
a very low resistance and be connected in series
questions.e: It must draw almost no current, so as not to disturb the circuit it measures.

questions.s: In a series LCR circuit R = 30 Ω, X_L = 60 Ω and X_C = 20 Ω. The impedance is
questions.e: Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²) = √(900 + 1,600) = 50 Ω. Adding the three values gives 110 Ω.

questions.s: A permanent magnet is moved towards a closed copper ring. The induced current in the ring
o: aids the motion of the magnet
flows only after the magnet stops
opposes the motion of the magnet
questions.e: By Lenz's law, the ring's field repels the approaching pole, so work must be done to push the magnet in. That work becomes the electrical energy.

questions.s: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. The magnetic field at a distance of 5 cm from it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
questions.e: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10/(2π × 0.05) = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T. Dropping the 2 from 2πr gives 8 × 10⁻⁵ T, and dropping the whole 2π gives 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ T.

questions.s: A torque acts on a current-carrying rectangular coil in a uniform magnetic field. The torque is greatest when the plane of the coil is
o: at rest at the neutral position
questions.e: τ = NBIA cosα for α the angle between the plane and the field, which is maximum when the plane is parallel to B. Perpendicular gives zero torque.

questions.s: In the household wiring, a fuse is placed in the
questions.e: The fuse must cut the live supply if too much current flows, so the appliance is left at no dangerous potential.

questions.s: The area enclosed by a hysteresis loop of a ferromagnetic material represents
o: energy lost as heat per unit volume per cycle
questions.e: Each cycle of magnetisation transfers energy to the material as heat. Soft iron, used in transformer cores, has a thin loop for this reason.

questions.s: The energy stored in a 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V is
questions.e: U = ½CV² = ½ × 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 0.05 J. Without the ½ the value would be 0.1 J, and 0.5 J comes from a slip of a power of ten.

questions.s: A 2 kW heater is run for 5 hours. The electrical energy used is
questions.e: Energy = power × time = 2 kW × 5 h = 10 kWh. Adding the two numbers gives 7, which is not energy.

questions.s: The potential at a point due to several point charges is found by
o: subtracting the largest from the smallest
questions.e: Potential is a scalar, so contributions simply add with their signs. Fields, being vectors, must be added vectorially.

questions.s: An electron moving at 2 × 10⁶ m/s enters at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.5 T. The magnitude of the force on it is
questions.e: F = qvB sin90° = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁶ × 0.5 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N. Leaving out the speed gives 8.0 × 10⁻²⁰ N, and no factor of ½ appears in the formula.

questions.s: A step-up transformer
o: has more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary
has fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary
questions.e: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. It raises voltage and reduces current, while an ideal one leaves power unchanged.

questions.s: An ideal transformer has 1,000 turns in the primary and 50 turns in the secondary. If the primary is connected to 220 V AC, the secondary voltage is
questions.e: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = 220 × 50/1,000 = 11 V. 4,400 V would arise from inverting the turns ratio.

questions.s: A long solenoid has 1,000 turns per metre and carries a current of 2 A. The magnetic field inside it is approximately (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
questions.e: B = μ₀nI = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1,000 × 2 = 2.51 × 10⁻³ T. Using the total length is not needed because n is already per metre.

questions.s: A parallel-plate air capacitor has plates of area 0.01 m² separated by 1 mm. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m, its capacitance is
questions.e: C = ε₀A/d = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.01/10⁻³ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹¹ F = 88.5 pF. Misreading mm as cm shifts the answer by a factor of ten.

questions.s: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, its kinetic energy gained is
questions.e: The energy gained is qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 100 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ J (100 eV). The energy for a 1 V difference would be only 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and 100 J forgets the electron charge.

questions.s: A point charge of 4 nC is placed in air. The electric field strength at a distance of 30 cm from it is
questions.e: E = kq/r² = 9 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻⁹/0.09 = 400 N/C. 120 is the potential in volts (kq/r), not a field.

questions.s: A wire is stretched uniformly until its length doubles, with its volume unchanged. Its resistance becomes
questions.e: R = ρL/A. With volume fixed, doubling L halves A, so R becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times larger. Twice is true only if the area stayed the same.

questions.s: The drift velocity of free electrons in a copper wire carrying a typical current is
o: close to the speed of light
very small, of the order of millimetres per second
questions.e: Electrons drift slowly, yet the electric field spreads at nearly the speed of light, so a bulb lights immediately.

questions.s: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is greatest when the conductor is
o: at right angles to the field
questions.e: F = BIL sinθ is maximum at θ = 90°; it is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.

questions.s: A 0.4 m straight wire carrying 5 A lies at right angles to a uniform field of 0.2 T. The force on it is
questions.e: F = BIL = 0.2 × 5 × 0.4 = 0.4 N. Dividing by the length gives the incorrect 2.5.

questions.s: If the distance between two point charges is doubled, the electrostatic force between them becomes
questions.e: F ∝ 1/r², so doubling r divides F by 4. Halving would be for an inverse proportion.

questions.s: To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, one must connect
o: a high resistance in series with it
a low resistance in parallel with it
a high resistance in parallel with it
a low resistance in series with it
questions.e: A shunt carries most of the current, so the meter is protected and has a small total resistance. A high series resistance makes a voltmeter.

questions.s: With rising temperature, the resistance of a pure semiconductor generally
questions.e: More charge carriers are freed at higher temperature, so conductivity rises. For metals the opposite occurs, as lattice vibrations increase.

questions.s: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the two resistors in one ratio arm are 10 Ω and 20 Ω, and a 30 Ω resistor lies next to the 10 Ω resistor. The fourth resistor, next to the 20 Ω resistor, must be
questions.e: At balance, 10/20 = 30/x, so x = 60 Ω. Inverting the ratio gives 15 Ω.

questions.s: Inside a charged hollow conductor, in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field is
o: equal to the field at the surface
questions.e: Free charges rearrange until the field inside the conducting material is zero, so a hollow cavity is shielded. This is how a Faraday cage works.

questions.s: For a 4 nC point charge in air, the electric potential at 30 cm from it is
questions.e: V = kq/r = 9 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻⁹/0.3 = 120 V. Using r² in the denominator gives the field value 400.

questions.s: The device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy is a
questions.e: A generator turns a coil in a field, inducing an emf. A motor does the reverse.

questions.s: Eddy currents in a transformer core are reduced by
questions.e: Thin insulated sheets raise the resistance in the paths of the induced currents. A solid core has large loops and big losses.

questions.s: Capacitors of 6 μF and 3 μF are connected in series. Their equivalent capacitance is
questions.e: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so C = 2 μF. The sum 9 μF applies to a parallel connection.

questions.s: The work done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface is
questions.e: No potential difference exists between points on the surface, so W = qΔV = 0. The field is perpendicular to such a surface.

questions.s: Self-inductance of a coil is
o: the resistance of the coil to direct current
the energy lost in the core
the property by which a coil opposes a change in its own current
questions.e: A changing current produces changing flux, and the induced emf opposes the change. Its unit is the henry.

questions.s: Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of
questions.e: An induced current opposes the change that causes it, otherwise energy could be created from nothing.

questions.s: A pure inductor of 0.1 H is connected to a 50 Hz AC supply. Its inductive reactance is approximately
questions.e: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.1 = 31.4 Ω. Using ω = 2πf = 314 without multiplying by L gives 314.

questions.s: Two point charges of +2 μC and +3 μC are placed 30 cm apart in air. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², the force between them is
questions.e: F = kq₁q₂/r² = 9 × 10⁹ × 6 × 10⁻¹² / 0.09 = 0.6 N. Like charges repel. Using r = 30 without converting to metres, or squaring wrongly, changes the magnitude.

questions.s: Which expression gives the average power in an AC circuit?
questions.e: Only the in-phase component of the current delivers net power; cosφ is the power factor. A pure inductor or capacitor has cosφ = 0 and uses no average power.

questions.s: A copper coil has a resistance of 100 Ω at 0 °C. If its temperature coefficient of resistance is 0.004 K⁻¹, its resistance at 50 °C is
questions.e: R = R₀(1 + αΔT) = 100 × (1 + 0.004 × 50) = 120 Ω. 104 Ω results from using α × 1 instead of α × 50.

questions.s: Resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. Their equivalent resistance is
questions.e: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω, which is less than the smaller resistor. 9 Ω is the series total.

questions.s: A rod of length 0.4 m moves at 5 m/s at right angles to a uniform field of 0.5 T and to its own length. The emf induced across it is
questions.e: ε = Blv = 0.5 × 0.4 × 5 = 1 V. Multiplying by an extra 5 (not dividing) gives 12.5.

questions.s: Electric field lines
o: can cross at the point of strongest field
form closed loops around positive charges
questions.e: The field at any point has a single direction, so two lines cannot cross. Lines begin on positive charges and end on negative ones.

questions.s: A material that is weakly repelled by a magnetic field is called
questions.e: Diamagnetic materials such as bismuth and copper develop an induced field that opposes the applied one. Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted.

questions.s: Kirchhoff's current law is a statement of the conservation of
questions.e: The total current entering a junction equals the total leaving, as charge cannot pile up. The voltage law expresses conservation of energy.

questions.s: A capacitor stores a charge of 60 μC when connected to a 12 V supply. Its capacitance is
questions.e: C = Q/V = 60/12 = 5 μF. Multiplying Q and V gives 720, which is not a capacitance.

questions.s: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω are connected in series across a 20 V supply. The current in the circuit is
questions.e: R = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω, so I = 20/10 = 2 A. 6.7 A uses the 3 Ω resistor alone, and 10 A is the total resistance.

questions.s: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a resistor of 4 Ω. The current is
questions.e: I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A. 0.33 A results from inverting the ratio.

questions.s: A bulb is marked 220 V, 100 W. Its resistance when it is working normally is
questions.e: P = V²/R gives R = 220²/100 = 484 Ω. 2.2 is V/P and 0.45 is I = P/V in amperes.

questions.s: A coil of 100 turns experiences a change in magnetic flux from 0.02 Wb to zero in 0.5 s. The average induced emf is
questions.e: ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 0.02/0.5 = 4 V. Forgetting the number of turns gives 0.04 V.

questions.s: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to an external resistor of 5 Ω. The terminal potential difference is
questions.e: I = 12/(5 + 1) = 2 A, and the terminal voltage is V = IR = 2 × 5 = 10 V (or 12 − 2 × 1). Terminal voltage equals the emf only when no current flows.

questions.s: Gauss's law states that the net electric flux through a closed surface is proportional to
o: the net charge enclosed by the surface
questions.e: Φ = Q/ε₀. Charges outside the surface contribute equal flux in and out, so the net is zero.

questions.s: A series circuit has L = 0.1 H and C = 10 μF. Its resonant frequency is approximately
questions.e: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(10⁻⁶)) = 1/(2π × 10⁻³) = 159 Hz. 1,000 rad/s is ω₀, and dividing by 2π converts it to hertz.

questions.s: Two parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. The force between them is
o: attractive only if the currents differ
questions.e: Each wire's field produces a force towards the other, so the wires attract. Opposite currents repel.

questions.s: The SI unit of electric field strength is
questions.e: E = F/q, so the unit is N/C (equivalently V/m). Joule per coulomb is the volt, the unit of potential.

questions.s: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is
questions.e: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so the angle between the two rays is 35° + 35° = 70°. 55° is the angle between the incident ray and the mirror surface.

questions.s: Light passes from air into glass of refractive index 1.5 with an angle of incidence of 45°. The angle of refraction is about
questions.e: Snell's law: sin r = sin 45°/1.5 = 0.7071/1.5 = 0.471, so r ≈ 28.1°. 30° would need sin r = 0.5, and 32° comes from dividing the angle itself (45°/1.5 = 30°) and rounding off.

questions.s: The critical angle for a glass–air boundary is found for glass of refractive index 1.5 to be about
questions.e: sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C ≈ 41.8°. 48° is the angle whose cosine is 0.667, and 56° is the angle whose tangent is 1.5.

questions.s: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image is formed at
o: 15 cm in front of the mirror
7.5 cm in front of the mirror
30 cm in front of the mirror
questions.e: With u = −30 cm and f = −10 cm, 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/10 + 1/30 = −1/15, so v = −15 cm. The negative sign means a real image in front of the mirror.

questions.s: An object is placed 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. The image distance is
questions.e: Using 1/v − 1/u = 1/f with u = −30 cm: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so v = 60 cm on the far side. 12 cm results from adding the reciprocals 1/20 + 1/30 by mistake.

questions.s: The power of a convex lens of focal length 25 cm is
questions.e: P = 1/f with f in metres: 1/0.25 = +4 dioptres. Using centimetres gives 0.04 D, and a convex lens has positive power.

questions.s: A real object stands 30 cm from a concave (diverging) lens of focal length 15 cm. The image is
o: real, inverted, 30 cm from the lens
virtual, upright, 10 cm from the lens
virtual, upright, 30 cm from the lens
real, inverted, 10 cm from the lens
questions.e: With f = −15 cm and u = −30 cm: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = −1/15 − 1/30 = −1/10, so v = −10 cm. A diverging lens always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image on the object's side.

questions.s: A man stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. The distance between him and his image is
questions.e: A plane mirror forms the image as far behind it as the object is in front, so the separation is 2 + 2 = 4 m. 2 m is only the distance to the mirror.

questions.s: Taking the speed of light in air as 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, its speed in glass of refractive index 1.5 is
questions.e: v = c/n = 3.0 × 10⁸/1.5 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Multiplying by n would wrongly make light faster than c.

questions.s: In Young's double-slit experiment the slit separation is 0.50 mm, the screen is 1.0 m away and the wavelength is 600 nm. The fringe spacing is
questions.e: Fringe width β = λD/d = 600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.0/(0.50 × 10⁻³) = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m. 0.83 mm is simply 1/1.2, the result of inverting the answer.

questions.s: In a double-slit experiment λ = 500 nm, the slit separation is 1.0 mm and the screen is 2.0 m away. The distance of the fourth dark fringe from the central maximum is
questions.e: β = λD/d = 1.0 mm. The dark fringes lie at (n − ½)β, so the fourth is at 3.5β = 3.5 mm. 4.0 mm is the position of the fourth bright fringe.

questions.s: Two coherent waves meet at a point on a screen. Constructive interference occurs there when the path difference is
o: an odd number of half wavelengths
an odd number of quarter wavelengths
questions.e: Waves arrive in phase when the path difference is 0, λ, 2λ, … giving a bright fringe. An odd number of half-wavelengths puts the waves in antiphase and gives darkness.

questions.s: A diffraction grating has a slit spacing of 2.0 μm. The highest order of a spectrum that can be seen with light of wavelength 600 nm is
questions.e: For a maximum, d sin θ = mλ, and sin θ cannot exceed 1: m ≤ 2,000/600 = 3.33, so m = 3. A fourth order would need sin θ = 1.2, which is impossible.

questions.s: Total internal reflection can occur only when light
o: travels from a rarer to a denser medium at any angle of incidence
travels from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
travels from a denser to a rarer medium at normal incidence
travels from a rarer to a denser medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
questions.e: Total internal reflection needs light to go from a higher to a lower refractive index, with the incidence angle beyond the critical angle. Light entering a denser medium always refracts.

questions.s: A simple microscope has a lens of focal length 5 cm. Taking the near point as 25 cm, its angular magnification when the image is formed at the near point is
questions.e: M = 1 + D/f = 1 + 25/5 = 6. The value 5 is D/f, which is the magnification for an image at infinity.

questions.s: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. In normal adjustment its angular magnification is
questions.e: In normal adjustment M = f_o/f_e = 100/5 = 20 and the lens separation is 105 cm. 105 is that separation, not the magnification.

questions.s: Unpolarised light is reflected from a glass surface of refractive index √3 at the polarising (Brewster) angle. This angle is
questions.e: Brewster's law: tan θ_p = n = √3, so θ_p = 60°. 30° is its complement, the angle of refraction at that incidence.

questions.s: Two thin convex lenses of focal lengths 20 cm and 30 cm are placed in contact. The focal length of the combination is
questions.e: For lenses in contact 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ = 1/20 + 1/30 = 5/60, so f = 12 cm. 25 cm is the simple average, which has no basis.

questions.s: A pond is 3.0 m deep and its water has refractive index 4/3. Viewed from directly above, its bottom appears to be at a depth of
questions.e: Apparent depth = real depth/n = 3.0 ÷ (4/3) = 2.25 m. Multiplying by n gives 4.0 m, which would make the pond look deeper, the opposite of what happens.

questions.s: A prism of angle 60° has a refractive index of √2. The angle of minimum deviation is
questions.e: n = sin[(A + D)/2]/sin(A/2): sin[(60° + D)/2] = √2 × 0.5 = 0.707, so (60° + D)/2 = 45° and D = 30°. 45° is half of the sum, not the deviation.

questions.s: A short-sighted person has a far point of 50 cm. The power of the lens that lets the person see distant objects clearly is
questions.e: The lens must form a virtual image at 50 cm of an object at infinity, so f = −50 cm = −0.5 m and P = 1/f = −2.0 D. A diverging lens is needed for short sight.

questions.s: The image formed by a convex mirror of a real object is always
questions.e: A convex mirror diverges the reflected rays, so the image seems to lie behind the mirror, and it is always smaller than the object. This is why it is used as a rear-view mirror.

questions.s: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5. Its wavelength in the glass is
questions.e: The frequency stays the same while the speed falls, so λ′ = λ/n = 600/1.5 = 400 nm. 900 nm would result from multiplying by n.

questions.s: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls on a single slit 0.20 mm wide. The angle (in radians) of the first minimum is approximately
questions.e: The first minimum satisfies a sin θ = λ, so θ ≈ 500 × 10⁻⁹/0.20 × 10⁻³ = 2.5 × 10⁻³ rad. A slit width in millimetres without conversion gives the 10⁻⁶ error.

questions.s: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. Its focal length is
questions.e: For a spherical mirror f = R/2 = 20 cm. 80 cm doubles instead of halving.

questions.s: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polaroid, and the emerging polarised light then passes through a second polaroid whose axis is at 60° to the first. The intensity finally emerging is
questions.e: The first polaroid halves the intensity to I₀/2. By Malus's law the second transmits cos² 60° = ¼ of that, giving I₀/8. I₀/4 forgets the first polaroid.

questions.s: The working of an optical fibre depends on the principle of
questions.e: Light inside the glass core meets the boundary with the lower-index cladding at angles beyond the critical angle and is reflected repeatedly along the fibre.

questions.s: A biconvex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.5, with both surfaces of radius of curvature 20 cm. Its focal length is
questions.e: Lens-maker's formula: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) = 0.5 × (1/20 + 1/20) = 1/20, so f = 20 cm. 40 cm results from using only one surface.

questions.s: A concave mirror of focal length 10 cm forms an image of an object placed 15 cm in front of it. The linear magnification is
questions.e: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u gives v = −30 cm in the sign convention; m = −v/u = −(−30)/(−15) = −2, so the image is real, inverted and twice the size. +2 would describe an upright image.

questions.s: In a Young's double-slit set-up in air the fringe width is 1.2 mm. The whole apparatus is then immersed in water of refractive index 4/3. The new fringe width is
questions.e: In water λ becomes λ/n, and β = λD/d is proportional to λ, so β′ = 1.2 × 3/4 = 0.90 mm. 1.6 mm multiplies by n, which is the wrong direction.

questions.s: Light of photon energy 3.5 eV falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is
questions.e: Einstein's equation: KE_max = hf − φ = 3.5 − 2.0 = 1.5 eV. 5.5 eV adds the work function instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: Taking h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, the threshold frequency of a metal with work function 2.0 eV is
questions.e: f₀ = φ/h = (2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The answer 4.8 × 10¹⁵ Hz comes from an error of a power of ten in the work function.

questions.s: With h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the energy of a photon of wavelength 500 nm is about
Photons of energy 4.5 eV fall on a metal whose work function is 2.5 eV. The stopping potential needed to stop the fastest photoelectrons is
questions.e: eV_s = KE_max = 4.5 − 2.5 = 2.0 eV, so V_s = 2.0 V. 2.5 V is the work function expressed in volts, which has no part in this answer.

questions.s: In the photoelectric effect, when the intensity of light of fixed frequency above the threshold is increased, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons
questions.e: The maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency, not the intensity. A higher intensity means more photons per second and so more photoelectrons, not faster ones.

questions.s: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. Its de Broglie wavelength is about
questions.e: λ = h/√(2meV) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/√(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 100) ≈ 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The handy form 1.23/√V nm gives the same value.

questions.s: A ball of mass 0.10 kg moves at 10 m/s. With h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, its de Broglie wavelength is
questions.e: λ = h/(mv) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.10 × 10) = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ m, far too small to detect, which is why everyday objects show no wave behaviour.

questions.s: According to the Bohr model, the energy of the electron in the second orbit (n = 2) of hydrogen is
questions.e: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, so E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV. −1.5 eV is the energy for n = 3, and −6.8 eV divides by n rather than n².

questions.s: A hydrogen atom drops from the n = 3 level to n = 2. The energy of the photon emitted is about
The energy needed to remove the electron from a hydrogen atom in its ground state is
questions.e: The ground state energy is −13.6 eV, so 13.6 eV must be supplied to ionise the atom. 27.2 eV is double the correct value.

questions.s: Taking the Rydberg constant as 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, the longest wavelength in the Lyman series of hydrogen is about
questions.e: For n = 2 → 1, 1/λ = R(1 − 1/4) = 0.75 × 1.097 × 10⁷, so λ ≈ 1.215 × 10⁻⁷ m. 656 nm is the first Balmer line, and 91 nm is the shortest Lyman wavelength.

questions.s: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is 0.529 Å. The radius of the third orbit is about
questions.e: rₙ = n²r₁ = 9 × 0.529 = 4.76 Å. 1.59 Å results from multiplying by n instead of n².

questions.s: Electrons accelerated through 20 kV strike a target and produce X-rays. Using hc = 1,240 eV nm, the minimum wavelength is
questions.e: All the electron's energy goes into one photon: λ_min = hc/eV = 1,240/20,000 = 0.062 nm. 0.62 nm has a misplaced decimal point.

questions.s: An alpha particle consists of
questions.e: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus with mass number 4 and atomic number 2, so it has 2 protons and 4 − 2 = 2 neutrons.

questions.s: When a nucleus undergoes β⁻ decay, its
o: atomic number decreases by 1 and mass number is unchanged
atomic number is unchanged and mass number decreases by 1
atomic number increases by 1 and mass number is unchanged
atomic number decreases by 2 and mass number decreases by 4
questions.e: In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton and emits an electron and an antineutrino, so Z rises by 1 while A stays the same. The last option describes alpha decay.

questions.s: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) emits one alpha particle. The daughter nucleus is
questions.e: Alpha emission lowers A by 4 and Z by 2: 238 − 4 = 234 and 92 − 2 = 90. Check: 234 + 4 = 238 and 90 + 2 = 92.

questions.s: A radioactive sample of mass 80 g has a half-life of 4 days. The mass of the original isotope left after 12 days is
questions.e: 12 days is 12/4 = 3 half-lives, so 80 × (½)³ = 10 g. 26.7 g divides by 3 as though decay were linear.

questions.s: What percentage of a radioactive sample remains undecayed after three half-lives?
questions.e: After each half-life the amount halves: 100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5 %. 6.25 % is the value after four half-lives.

questions.s: A radioisotope has a half-life of 10 minutes. Its decay constant is about
questions.e: λ = ln 2/T½ = 0.693/10 = 0.0693 min⁻¹. 14.4 min⁻¹ is the reciprocal, T½/ln 2, which is the mean life in minutes.

questions.s: The mass defect of a nucleus is 0.030 u. Taking 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², the binding energy is about
questions.e: E = Δm c² = 0.030 × 931.5 = 27.9 MeV. 0.28 MeV loses two powers of ten.

questions.s: The mass of a helium-4 nucleus is 4.0015 u, of a proton 1.0073 u and of a neutron 1.0087 u. With 1 u = 931.5 MeV, the binding energy per nucleon is about
questions.e: Δm = 2(1.0073) + 2(1.0087) − 4.0015 = 0.0305 u, so B = 0.0305 × 931.5 ≈ 28.4 MeV. Dividing by the 4 nucleons gives about 7.1 MeV; 28 MeV is the total, not the value per nucleon.

questions.s: Taking c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the energy equivalent of a mass of 1.0 g is
questions.e: E = mc² = 1.0 × 10⁻³ kg × (3.0 × 10⁸)² = 9.0 × 10¹³ J. Forgetting to convert grams to kilograms gives 9.0 × 10¹⁶ J.

questions.s: A semiconductor doped with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus is
o: p-type, with holes as the majority carriers
n-type, with electrons as the majority carriers
n-type, with holes as the majority carriers
p-type, with electrons as the majority carriers
questions.e: Each phosphorus atom has five valence electrons, one more than silicon needs for bonding, so free electrons become the majority carriers. The crystal remains electrically neutral.

questions.s: When a p–n junction diode is forward biased, the width of its depletion region
questions.e: Forward bias pushes holes and electrons towards the junction, narrowing the depletion layer and lowering the barrier so that current flows.

questions.s: A full-wave rectifier is supplied from a 50 Hz a.c. source. The frequency of the ripple in its output is
questions.e: A full-wave rectifier turns both half-cycles into pulses in the same direction, so there are two output pulses per input cycle: 2 × 50 = 100 Hz. A half-wave rectifier would leave it at 50 Hz.

questions.s: The output of a two-input NOR gate is 1 when
questions.e: NOR is OR followed by NOT. OR gives 0 only for inputs 0, 0, so NOR gives 1 only in that case.

questions.s: In a common-emitter transistor circuit the base current is 20 μA and the collector current is 2.0 mA. The current gain β is
questions.e: β = I_C/I_B = 2.0 × 10⁻³/20 × 10⁻⁶ = 100. 99 results from subtracting 1 for no reason, and 0.01 is the inverse ratio I_B/I_C.

questions.s: A transistor has current gain β = 50 and base current 0.10 mA. The emitter current is
questions.e: I_C = βI_B = 50 × 0.10 = 5.0 mA, and I_E = I_B + I_C = 5.1 mA. 5.0 mA ignores the base current, which also leaves through the emitter.

questions.s: A clock on a spacecraft moving at 0.6c records a time interval of 4.0 s between two events. For an observer on Earth the interval is
questions.e: The spacecraft clock measures the proper time. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.36) = 1.25, so the Earth observer measures 4.0 × 1.25 = 5.0 s. 3.2 s multiplies by 1/γ, which is the wrong direction.

questions.s: In a nuclear reactor, the purpose of the moderator, such as heavy water or graphite, is to
o: absorb neutrons to stop the chain reaction
questions.e: Slow (thermal) neutrons are much better at causing fission of uranium-235. Control rods, not the moderator, absorb neutrons.

questions.s: A photon has wavelength 500 nm. With h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, its momentum is
questions.e: p = h/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(500 × 10⁻⁹) = 1.33 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s. 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the photon's energy in joules, a different quantity.

questions.s: The threshold wavelength of a metal for photoelectric emission is 500 nm. Using hc = 1,240 eV nm, its work function is about
questions.e: φ = hc/λ₀ = 1,240/500 = 2.48 eV. 0.4 eV inverts the ratio, giving λ₀/hc.

questions.s: In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the angular momentum of the electron in the n-th orbit is
questions.e: Bohr's quantisation condition is mvr = nh/2π, so the angular momentum comes only in whole-number multiples of h/2π.

questions.s: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the electron to that of the proton is about
questions.e: For the same KE, λ = h/√(2mK), so λ_e/λ_p = √(m_p/m_e) = √1,836 ≈ 43. 1,836 forgets the square root.

questions.s: A Zener diode is mainly used as a
questions.e: In reverse breakdown a Zener diode holds a nearly constant voltage across it over a wide range of current, which stabilises the supply.

questions.s: The output of a two-input OR gate is 0 when
questions.e: An OR gate gives 1 if at least one input is 1, so it gives 0 only when neither input is.

questions.s: The activity of a radioactive source falls from 1,600 counts per second to 100 counts per second in 12 hours. Its half-life is
questions.e: The activity has fallen by a factor of 16 = 2⁴, so four half-lives passed: T½ = 12/4 = 3 hours. 6 hours would suit a fall by a factor of 4.

questions.s: In β⁻ decay the electron emitted comes from
o: the conversion of a neutron into a proton inside the nucleus
the innermost orbit of the atom
the conversion of a proton into a neutron inside the nucleus
the splitting of an alpha particle
questions.e: The nucleus does not contain electrons; a neutron changes into a proton, and an electron and an antineutrino are created and emitted.

questions.s: The energy required to raise the electron in a hydrogen atom from n = 1 to n = 3 is about
questions.e: ΔE = 13.6(1/1² − 1/3²) = 13.6 × 8/9 = 12.09 eV. 10.2 eV is the energy for n = 1 → 2 only.

questions.s: A rod has a proper length of 1.00 m. It moves lengthways past an observer at 0.8c. The length the observer measures is
questions.e: Length contraction: L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²) = 1.00 × √(1 − 0.64) = 0.60 m. 1.67 m would be an expansion, which relativity does not predict for lengths along the motion.
